The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships were the 58th edition of the annual global competition in cyclo-cross, organized by the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) and held on 27–28 January 2007 at the Domenico Savio park in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium.[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2) This event featured races across elite, under-23, and junior categories for men and the elite category for women, contested on a technically demanding course with sandy sections, climbs, and barriers that drew approximately 30,000 spectators.[[1]](#ref-1)[[3]](#ref-3)
In the elite men's race on 28 January, defending champion Erwin Vervecken of Belgium secured his third world title in a time of 1:05:35, edging out Jonathan Page of the United States by three seconds for silver—the first-ever medal for a U.S. rider in the elite men's category—and Enrico Franzoi of Italy by 16 seconds for bronze.[[1]](#ref-1)[[3]](#ref-3) The race was marked by significant chaos, including a major crash caused by a television crew's quad bike dislodging a barrier, which eliminated favorites like Sven Nys (11th place) and affected others such as Richard Groenendaal (6th); additional incidents, including multiple falls and a collapsing fence due to crowd pressure, contributed to an unpredictable outcome.[[1]](#ref-1)
The elite women's event, also on 28 January, was won by Maryline Salvetat of France in 42:57, with American Katherine Compton taking silver just one second behind and French rider Laurence Leboucher claiming bronze nine seconds off the pace.[[4]](#ref-4) In the under-23 men's race on 27 January, Lars Boom of the Netherlands triumphed in 53:53, followed by Niels Albert of Belgium (1:22 back) and Romain Villa of France (1:44 back).[[5]](#ref-5) The junior men's race saw Belgian Joeri Adams victorious, with American Daniel Summerhill earning silver and Czech Jiri Polnicky bronze.[[6]](#ref-6) Overall, the championships highlighted Belgium's dominance with multiple medals, while the U.S. achieved a historic breakthrough with three medals across categories, underscoring the event's role in elevating cyclo-cross's international profile amid challenging weather and course conditions.[[1]](#ref-1)

## Background

### Historical Context

The UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships originated in 1950 with the inaugural event held in Charenton-le-Pont, near Paris, France, initially as an amateur competition open only to non-professional riders.[[7]](#ref-7) This marked the formal recognition of cyclo-cross as a distinct discipline under the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), the global governing body for cycling established in 1900, which has overseen the championships since their inception.[[7]](#ref-7) The event quickly gained traction in Europe, particularly in countries like Belgium, the Netherlands, and France, where the sport's demanding mix of road, off-road, and obstacle navigation resonated with local cycling traditions.[[8]](#ref-8) The elite women's category was introduced in 2000, expanding participation.[[9]](#ref-9)
By 1967, the championships evolved to include professional riders in the elite category, while a separate amateur men's event ran until 1993, reflecting the sport's growing professionalism and appeal beyond grassroots levels.[[9]](#ref-9) Key milestones included the introduction of the junior men's category in 1979 and the under-23 men's category in 1996, broadening participation and nurturing talent pathways within the UCI framework.[[9]](#ref-9) These changes coincided with enhanced UCI governance, formalized in the 1990s through structural reforms that unified amateur and professional bodies under a single entity by 1992, ensuring standardized rules and international expansion.[[7]](#ref-7) The championships are traditionally scheduled in January, aligning with the cyclo-cross season's winter peak to capitalize on challenging conditions like mud and frost.[[9]](#ref-9)
As the pinnacle of cyclo-cross, the World Championships hold immense prestige, testing riders' technical prowess on varied terrain—including grass, sand, and barriers—that demands frequent dismounts, bike handling, and endurance.[[8]](#ref-8) Historically, Belgian and Dutch riders have dominated, with Belgium securing over 20 gold medals across categories by the mid-2000s, underscoring the sport's cultural stronghold in these nations where national fervor and dense racing calendars fuel elite development.[[8]](#ref-8) This European-centric growth, bolstered by events in countries like the Czech Republic, positioned the championships as a global showcase by the mid-2000s, following the 2006 edition in Zeddam, Netherlands.[[8]](#ref-8)

### Host Selection and Preparation

The Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) selected Hooglede-Gits, Belgium, as the host for the 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships via a vote on January 31, 2004.[[10]](#ref-10)
The local organizing committee, Veldritcomité Hooglede-Gits, led by Rik Debeaussaert, coordinated preparations, focusing on infrastructure enhancements at Domenico Savio Park to accommodate approximately 30,000 spectators.[[11]](#ref-11)[[1]](#ref-1) Key upgrades included situating the venue adjacent to a railway station for improved accessibility and installing a double row of fences along the 3 km course to enhance rider safety and prevent spectator interference, a response to prior incidents at Belgian events.[[11]](#ref-11)
Preparatory efforts spanned from the 2004 announcement through late 2006, with course design emphasizing a mix of grass, forest sections, and a challenging 35-meter sand pit; the track was closed to training in the weeks leading up to the event to preserve conditions after heavy rainfall.[[11]](#ref-11) The committee operated on a budget of 1.2 million euros, facing a 250,000-euro shortfall that necessitated selling at least 20,000 tickets at 25 euros each for the elite races to achieve financial balance, with nearly 10,000 already sold two weeks prior.[[11]](#ref-11)
Challenges centered on the January timing in Flanders, where persistent wet weather risked creating muddy, treacherous conditions—particularly in the sand section, which former champion Roland Liboton predicted could prove decisive—and demanded robust planning for crowd management amid expectations of massive attendance.[[11]](#ref-11)

## Event Overview

### Location and Venue

The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships were held at Domenico Savio Park in Hooglede-Gits, a municipality in the province of West Flanders, Belgium.[[1]](#ref-1) The venue is situated at approximately 50°59′N 03°05′E, within the Flemish Region's characteristic flat to gently undulating agricultural landscape, which often provides ideal conditions for cyclo-cross with its potential for muddy and technical terrain.[[12]](#ref-12)[[13]](#ref-13)
Hooglede-Gits lies about 20 km northwest of Kortrijk, placing the park squarely in the heartland of Belgian cyclo-cross racing, where the sport has deep cultural roots and frequent high-level events occur nearby. The site's selection leveraged this proximity to draw strong local support, with facilities accommodating around 30,000 spectators over the weekend through designated viewing areas and organizational measures like fencing and stewards to manage crowds.[[1]](#ref-1)
The park's open, versatile grounds were well-suited to cyclo-cross demands, offering space for a challenging course that incorporated natural elements such as potential sand and elevation changes typical of Flemish parks, while minimizing disruption through pre-event planning for spectator access and vehicle parking.[[1]](#ref-1) This setup ensured the venue could host international competition effectively, highlighting Belgium's expertise in staging the discipline.

### Schedule and Course

The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships took place over two days, January 27 and 28, in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium.[[11]](#ref-11) The event followed the standard format for the discipline, with junior and under-23 men's races scheduled for Saturday and the elite women's and men's races on Sunday, allowing for progression from younger categories to the premier events.[[11]](#ref-11)
On Saturday, January 27, the junior men's race commenced in the morning, followed by the under-23 men's race in the afternoon.[[14]](#ref-14) Sunday, January 28, featured the elite women's race in the morning and the elite men's race in the afternoon, with the championships concluding that evening.[[1]](#ref-1) This timing accommodated spectator attendance, with an estimated 30,000 people present across the weekend.[[1]](#ref-1)
The course was a 3-kilometer loop at Domenico Savio Park, designed with varied terrain to test riders' skills across multiple laps.[[11]](#ref-11) It primarily consisted of grass sections, a challenging 35-meter sand pit that often proved decisive, a technical forest area with roots and steep descents, and a run-up featuring stairs where riders typically shouldered their bikes.[[11]](#ref-11) Additional obstacles included barriers, corners prone to slipping, and short climbs, including a final uphill straight; double-row fences lined the entire route to manage crowds.[[1]](#ref-1) The layout emphasized bike handling over significant elevation gain, with no pre-event training allowed to preserve course integrity.[[11]](#ref-11)
Conditions reflected the typical cold, wet Flemish winter, following recent heavy rain that had softened the ground but left it relatively firm rather than a deep quagmire.[[11]](#ref-11)

## Participants

### Nations and Teams

The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships featured participants from approximately 20 nations across all categories, with a strong European dominance reflecting the sport's traditional strongholds.[[1]](#ref-1) Belgium, the host nation, fielded the largest contingent with over 20 riders spread across elite, under-23, junior, and women's events, followed closely by the Netherlands with around 20 athletes. Other prominent European nations included France (approximately 15 riders), Italy (15), Germany (12), Czech Republic (10), and Switzerland (8), while emerging non-European participants came from the United States (19 riders total) and Canada (7).[[1]](#ref-1)[[15]](#ref-15)[[16]](#ref-16)[[14]](#ref-14)
National teams were formed through selections based on UCI cyclo-cross rankings and domestic championships, with quotas restricting entries per nation—typically up to eight riders in the elite men's category for top-ranked countries like Belgium and the Netherlands, and fewer for others. The under-23 and junior categories allowed similar limits, often five to six per nation for leading teams, while women's entries were capped at around six for dominant federations. Smaller squads from nations like Japan (10 riders total), Poland (9), and Spain (8) highlighted growing global interest, though European teams accounted for over 80% of starters.[[1]](#ref-1)[[15]](#ref-15)
Logistics for international teams involved coordinated travel to Belgium, the event host, with many squads establishing pre-championship training camps in the region to acclimate to local conditions and courses. For instance, North American teams like the USA's utilized European preparation camps in late 2006 and early 2007 to optimize performance ahead of the January event.[[17]](#ref-17) These arrangements underscored the championships' role in fostering international participation, despite the logistical challenges for distant nations.

### Notable Riders

In the elite men's category, Sven Nys of Belgium entered as the overwhelming favorite, having led the UCI rankings and claimed the national championship with an unbeaten streak broken only eight times that season, all within the top five.[[11]](#ref-11) Defending world champion Erwin Vervecken, also Belgian, was seen as a strong contender despite a quieter season with just one major victory, relying on his tactical acumen and hoping for frozen conditions to level the field.[[11]](#ref-11) Bart Wellens, another Belgian national titleholder, brought renewed confidence from his domestic win, though his sensitivity to cold and wet weather raised questions about his endurance.[[11]](#ref-11) Dutch riders Gerben de Knegt and Richard Groenendaal represented non-Belgian hopes, with de Knegt viewed as a podium threat despite a recent abandonment, while Groenendaal aimed to end a seven-year Belgian stranglehold on the rainbow jersey.[[11]](#ref-11)
The elite women's field lacked a singular dominant force, setting up a highly competitive race with multiple medal possibilities.[[11]](#ref-11) Hanka Kupfernagel of Germany, the UCI points leader and national champion, was the preeminent favorite after securing the latest World Cup round in Hoogerheide, though her aversion to muddy conditions added intrigue.[[11]](#ref-11) Defending champion Marianne Vos of the Netherlands, at just 19, was highlighted as Kupfernagel's chief rival for her explosive sprint and emerging talent, despite a season limited to one World Cup victory.[[11]](#ref-11) French champion Maryline Salvetat and compatriot Laurence Leboucher were anticipated to challenge strongly, with Leboucher demonstrating championship pedigree by recently defeating Kupfernagel.[[11]](#ref-11) American Katie Compton, the U.S. national champion, arrived in solid form after dominating domestically and posting a top-10 in her last World Cup, marking her as a rising international prospect.[[11]](#ref-11)
Among the under-23 men, a intense rivalry brewed between Belgian Niels Albert and Dutch Lars Boom, both of whom had dominated recent elite-level races—Boom by winning the Dutch elite nationals against seasoned professionals, and Albert by triumphing over the full elite peloton in Loenhout.[[11]](#ref-11) Defending champion Zdenek Stybar of the Czech Republic lingered as a potential dark horse despite a dip in late-season results.[[11]](#ref-11) This matchup was billed as one of the weekend's most captivating, with both riders positioned as future stars of the sport.[[11]](#ref-11)
The junior men's race promised unpredictability with no runaway leader, though Belgian Joeri Adams stood out for his World Cup victory and consistent top finishes, poised to leverage fervent local support.[[11]](#ref-11) Czech Jiri Polnicky earned notice for his steady top-six placings across World Cup events, while compatriots Vincent Bastaens of Belgium and French duo Thomas Girard and Arnaud Jouffroy rounded out the key prospects.[[11]](#ref-11) American Danny Summerhill, the U.S. junior champion, added an international dimension as an emerging talent.[[11]](#ref-11)
Pre-event buzz centered on Belgium's home-soil advantage in Hooglede-Gits, where the nation—boasting nearly double the UCI points of rivals the Netherlands—anticipated reclaiming dominance after years without a non-Belgian elite men's victor.[[11]](#ref-11) Organizers expected record crowds of up to 20,000, amplified by the challenging course featuring a demanding sand section, with media spotlighting Flemish passion and national pressure on the Belgian contingent.[[11]](#ref-11) No significant injuries disrupted the field, though weather vulnerabilities for riders like Wellens heightened tactical discussions.[[11]](#ref-11)

## Men's Events

### Elite Race

The men's elite race at the 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships was held on 28 January in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium. Featuring a field of 50 riders from 18 nations, the event was contested on a 3 km technically demanding course with sandy sections, climbs, and barriers. The race lasted approximately 65 minutes and was marked by chaos, including a major crash caused by a television crew's quad bike and a collapsing barrier due to spectator pressure.[[1]](#ref-1)
Defending champion Erwin Vervecken of Belgium won in 1:05:35, securing his third world title. Jonathan Page of the United States took silver three seconds behind, marking the first medal for a U.S. rider in the elite men's category. Enrico Franzoi of Italy earned bronze 16 seconds back. Favorites like Sven Nys finished 11th after being affected by incidents, while Richard Groenendaal placed 6th.[[3]](#ref-3)

### Under-23 Race

The men's under-23 race at the 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships took place on 27 January 2007 in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium, serving as a key platform for youth development in the discipline. With a field of 57 riders from over 20 nations, the event emphasized international competition among riders aged 19 to 22, fostering emerging talents in a challenging cyclo-cross environment.[[5]](#ref-5)
Lars Boom of the Netherlands claimed the rainbow jersey, completing the muddy 3.05 km course in 53 minutes and 53 seconds over seven laps. Niels Albert from Belgium earned silver, crossing the line 1 minute and 22 seconds behind, while Romain Villa of France secured bronze, 1 minute and 44 seconds off Boom's pace. Fourth place went to Zdenek Stybar of the Czech Republic at +2'29", followed by Philipp Walsleben (Germany) at +2'49" and Lukas Kloucek (Czech Republic) at +2'56".[[18]](#ref-18)[[5]](#ref-5)
Boom's dominant performance highlighted a resurgence for Dutch cyclo-cross in the under-23 category, building on the nation's strong tradition in the sport. The race underscored the category's role in nurturing future stars, as evidenced by Albert's subsequent success; he went on to win the elite world title in 2012.[[19]](#ref-19)

### Junior Race

The junior men's race at the 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships, held on January 27 in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium, featured approximately 60 riders under the age of 19 competing over a shortened course adapted for the category's developmental focus, with the event lasting around 40 minutes.
Joeri Adams of Belgium claimed the world title in a winning time of 41:18.0, edging out Daniel Summerhill of the United States by 0.7 seconds for silver, while Jiri Polnicky of the Czech Republic secured bronze 1.3 seconds behind. The race unfolded with an early breakaway group of seven after the first lap, marked by Polnicky's aggressive attacks and Summerhill's recovery from a crash on a steep descent during the third lap. Entering the final lap, a lead group of four—Polnicky, Adams, Summerhill, and Ramon Sinkeldam of the Netherlands—remained together, setting up a tense bunch sprint on the uphill finish straight where Adams' local course knowledge and explosive kick proved decisive.

The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships were the 58th edition of the annual global competition in cyclo-cross, organized by the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) and held on 27–28 January 2007 at the Domenico Savio park in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium.[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2) This event featured races across elite, under-23, and junior categories for men and the elite category for women, contested on a technically demanding course with sandy sections, climbs, and barriers that drew approximately 30,000 spectators.[[1]](#ref-1)[[3]](#ref-3)
In the elite men's race on 28 January, defending champion Erwin Vervecken of Belgium secured his third world title in a time of 1:05:35, edging out Jonathan Page of the United States by three seconds for silver—the first-ever medal for a U.S. rider in the elite men's category—and Enrico Franzoi of Italy by 16 seconds for bronze.[[1]](#ref-1)[[3]](#ref-3) The race was marked by significant chaos, including a major crash caused by a television crew's quad bike dislodging a barrier, which eliminated favorites like Sven Nys (11th place) and affected others such as Richard Groenendaal (6th); additional incidents, including multiple falls and a collapsing fence due to crowd pressure, contributed to an unpredictable outcome.[[1]](#ref-1)
The elite women's event, also on 28 January, was won by Maryline Salvetat of France in 42:57, with American Katherine Compton taking silver just one second behind and French rider Laurence Leboucher claiming bronze nine seconds off the pace.[[4]](#ref-4) In the under-23 men's race on 27 January, Lars Boom of the Netherlands triumphed in 53:53, followed by Niels Albert of Belgium (1:22 back) and Romain Villa of France (1:44 back).[[5]](#ref-5) The junior men's race saw Belgian Joeri Adams victorious, with American Daniel Summerhill earning silver and Czech Jiri Polnicky bronze.[[6]](#ref-6) Overall, the championships highlighted Belgium's dominance with multiple medals, while the U.S. achieved a historic breakthrough with three medals across categories, underscoring the event's role in elevating cyclo-cross's international profile amid challenging weather and course conditions.[[1]](#ref-1)

## Background

### Historical Context

The UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships originated in 1950 with the inaugural event held in Charenton-le-Pont, near Paris, France, initially as an amateur competition open only to non-professional riders.[[7]](#ref-7) This marked the formal recognition of cyclo-cross as a distinct discipline under the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), the global governing body for cycling established in 1900, which has overseen the championships since their inception.[[7]](#ref-7) The event quickly gained traction in Europe, particularly in countries like Belgium, the Netherlands, and France, where the sport's demanding mix of road, off-road, and obstacle navigation resonated with local cycling traditions.[[8]](#ref-8) The elite women's category was introduced in 2000, expanding participation.[[9]](#ref-9)
By 1967, the championships evolved to include professional riders in the elite category, while a separate amateur men's event ran until 1993, reflecting the sport's growing professionalism and appeal beyond grassroots levels.[[9]](#ref-9) Key milestones included the introduction of the junior men's category in 1979 and the under-23 men's category in 1996, broadening participation and nurturing talent pathways within the UCI framework.[[9]](#ref-9) These changes coincided with enhanced UCI governance, formalized in the 1990s through structural reforms that unified amateur and professional bodies under a single entity by 1992, ensuring standardized rules and international expansion.[[7]](#ref-7) The championships are traditionally scheduled in January, aligning with the cyclo-cross season's winter peak to capitalize on challenging conditions like mud and frost.[[9]](#ref-9)
As the pinnacle of cyclo-cross, the World Championships hold immense prestige, testing riders' technical prowess on varied terrain—including grass, sand, and barriers—that demands frequent dismounts, bike handling, and endurance.[[8]](#ref-8) Historically, Belgian and Dutch riders have dominated, with Belgium securing over 20 gold medals across categories by the mid-2000s, underscoring the sport's cultural stronghold in these nations where national fervor and dense racing calendars fuel elite development.[[8]](#ref-8) This European-centric growth, bolstered by events in countries like the Czech Republic, positioned the championships as a global showcase by the mid-2000s, following the 2006 edition in Zeddam, Netherlands.[[8]](#ref-8)

### Host Selection and Preparation

The Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) selected Hooglede-Gits, Belgium, as the host for the 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships via a vote on January 31, 2004.[[10]](#ref-10)
The local organizing committee, Veldritcomité Hooglede-Gits, led by Rik Debeaussaert, coordinated preparations, focusing on infrastructure enhancements at Domenico Savio Park to accommodate approximately 30,000 spectators.[[11]](#ref-11)[[1]](#ref-1) Key upgrades included situating the venue adjacent to a railway station for improved accessibility and installing a double row of fences along the 3 km course to enhance rider safety and prevent spectator interference, a response to prior incidents at Belgian events.[[11]](#ref-11)
Preparatory efforts spanned from the 2004 announcement through late 2006, with course design emphasizing a mix of grass, forest sections, and a challenging 35-meter sand pit; the track was closed to training in the weeks leading up to the event to preserve conditions after heavy rainfall.[[11]](#ref-11) The committee operated on a budget of 1.2 million euros, facing a 250,000-euro shortfall that necessitated selling at least 20,000 tickets at 25 euros each for the elite races to achieve financial balance, with nearly 10,000 already sold two weeks prior.[[11]](#ref-11)
Challenges centered on the January timing in Flanders, where persistent wet weather risked creating muddy, treacherous conditions—particularly in the sand section, which former champion Roland Liboton predicted could prove decisive—and demanded robust planning for crowd management amid expectations of massive attendance.[[11]](#ref-11)

## Event Overview

### Location and Venue

The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships were held at Domenico Savio Park in Hooglede-Gits, a municipality in the province of West Flanders, Belgium.[[1]](#ref-1) The venue is situated at approximately 50°59′N 03°05′E, within the Flemish Region's characteristic flat to gently undulating agricultural landscape, which often provides ideal conditions for cyclo-cross with its potential for muddy and technical terrain.[[12]](#ref-12)[[13]](#ref-13)
Hooglede-Gits lies about 20 km northwest of Kortrijk, placing the park squarely in the heartland of Belgian cyclo-cross racing, where the sport has deep cultural roots and frequent high-level events occur nearby. The site's selection leveraged this proximity to draw strong local support, with facilities accommodating around 30,000 spectators over the weekend through designated viewing areas and organizational measures like fencing and stewards to manage crowds.[[1]](#ref-1)
The park's open, versatile grounds were well-suited to cyclo-cross demands, offering space for a challenging course that incorporated natural elements such as potential sand and elevation changes typical of Flemish parks, while minimizing disruption through pre-event planning for spectator access and vehicle parking.[[1]](#ref-1) This setup ensured the venue could host international competition effectively, highlighting Belgium's expertise in staging the discipline.

### Schedule and Course

The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships took place over two days, January 27 and 28, in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium.[[11]](#ref-11) The event followed the standard format for the discipline, with junior and under-23 men's races scheduled for Saturday and the elite women's and men's races on Sunday, allowing for progression from younger categories to the premier events.[[11]](#ref-11)
On Saturday, January 27, the junior men's race commenced in the morning, followed by the under-23 men's race in the afternoon.[[14]](#ref-14) Sunday, January 28, featured the elite women's race in the morning and the elite men's race in the afternoon, with the championships concluding that evening.[[1]](#ref-1) This timing accommodated spectator attendance, with an estimated 30,000 people present across the weekend.[[1]](#ref-1)
The course was a 3-kilometer loop at Domenico Savio Park, designed with varied terrain to test riders' skills across multiple laps.[[11]](#ref-11) It primarily consisted of grass sections, a challenging 35-meter sand pit that often proved decisive, a technical forest area with roots and steep descents, and a run-up featuring stairs where riders typically shouldered their bikes.[[11]](#ref-11) Additional obstacles included barriers, corners prone to slipping, and short climbs, including a final uphill straight; double-row fences lined the entire route to manage crowds.[[1]](#ref-1) The layout emphasized bike handling over significant elevation gain, with no pre-event training allowed to preserve course integrity.[[11]](#ref-11)
Conditions reflected the typical cold, wet Flemish winter, following recent heavy rain that had softened the ground but left it relatively firm rather than a deep quagmire.[[11]](#ref-11)

### Nations and Teams

The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships featured participants from approximately 20 nations across all categories, with a strong European dominance reflecting the sport's traditional strongholds.[[1]](#ref-1) Belgium, the host nation, fielded the largest contingent with over 20 riders spread across elite, under-23, junior, and women's events, followed closely by the Netherlands with around 20 athletes. ### Race 1 - January 27: Juniors

### Adams kicks off the Belgian path to glory

#### Summerhill crashs but battled for the medal

By Brecht Decaluw� in Hooglede-Gits

 Adams tops podium

 Photo ©: Brecht Decaluw�

 /photos/2007/jan07/CXworlds07/index.php?id=/photos/2007/jan07/CXworlds07/CXworlds071/bd115905

World Cup winner Joeri Adams fulfilled the expectations by becoming the new
 junior world champion. The Belgian didn't dominate the race and had to wait
 for the final straight before he could hammer down to take the title. The Belgian
 beat American Danny Summerhill and Czech Jiri Polnicky in a sprint with four,
 Dutch Ramon Sinkeldam had to settle for the least wanted position just outside
 of the podium.

The Belgian explained he made mistake during the last lap, "I was only in fourth position at the stairs but by taking the corner wide I could still win the sprint. Anyway you know that at the worlds the speed will drop in front. I wasn't afraid to let it come down to a sprint, although I didn't know if I was the fastest of the group. The slightly upward final straight was in my advantage," Adams reflected.

The Belgian winner often switched bikes, a manoeuvre which was exploited by the Czech rider Polnicky who always attacked at the same moment. "I changed my bike intentionally during the second lap, I wanted a lighter bike. But during the third lap I think I took the corner a bit too wide so I ended up into the pits again," Adams explained about his unintentional tactics. Two riders ended up into the pits as well but didn't change bikes, they were disqualified.

Summerhill was beaten by the Belgian in the final straight and appeared disappointed with that place. "Actually I wasn't, I was happy to prove America could do something," Summerhill laughed while talking to Cyclingnews. "I didn't think I could make it to the sprint finish after my crash. Maybe if I played the sprint a bit differently, but you got to be happy with a medal as it is a good result."

Jiri Polnicky was the most aggressive rider out there in Flanders' fields but eventually he had to settle for third. "I'm not good at the finish so I tried to get away in technical sectors but it didn't work out like that," Polnicky said.

#### How it unfolded

A great start for the Italians when Calderan managed to get a gap during the
 first half of the course. American Danny Summerhill took the initiative to bridge
 up towards the Italians. By the end of the first lap Calderan was followed by
 a group of seven with Jiri Polnicky (Czech Republic), Ole Quast (Germany), Danny
 Summerhill (USA), Joeri Adams (Belgium), Ramon Sinkeldam (Netherlands), Arnaud
 Jouffroy (France) and a Polish rider.

During the second lap Polnicky � third in the World Cup � attacked the group
 but in the sand section of 35 metres; Polnicky needed to step off his bike,
 while World Cup winner Adams kept pedalling to close the gap.

Halfway through the second lap some riders decided to switch bikes, and just
 at that moment Polnicky attacked again. By the end of the second lap the Czech
 rider had a gap of eight seconds on a group of five, with Summerhill, Adams,
 Sinkeldam, Jouffroy and Quast. The Dutchman closed the gap to the Czech rider
 and by the end of the third lap five riders were back together, while Jouffroy
 was eight seconds behind this group.

During the third lap Summerhill crashed on a steep descent dropping back to
 Jouffroy; the Colorado-based rider didn�t give up, and together with the French
 rider he fought his way back to the front group. On the long uphill section
 in the forest, Adams was the only rider that stayed on his bike, sending out
 a warning to his rivals. The French champion suffered in the sand section and
 he got dropped again. Going into the ultimate lap it was clear that five riders
 would battle for the victory; Jouffroy was eleven seconds down.

Polnicky led the group during the first half of the ultimate lap, keeping the
 pace high. Sinkeldam attacked the group on the first climb with Polnicky and
 Summerhill not too far behind. The Dutchman survived the sand section and looked
 to be speeding towards a world title. During the last climb Polnicky closed
 the gap but Adams and Summerhill followed. It came down to a sprint where Adams
 overtook everybody, beating Summerhill, Polnicky and Sinkeldam. German Quast
 came in fifth and Jouffrouy seventh. Quick starter Calderan finished eighth.
